newsitem.title: SPAIN: U.S. and Spain air differences on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and Spain air differences on Cuba.

text.p: Spain aired its differences with Washington over Cuba on Sunday, rejecting the U.S. economic embargo and legislation targeting foreign investment in the Caribbean island.

U.S. ambassador to Spain Richard Gardner, seated beside U.S. Secretary of Transportation Federico Pena, defended his government's policy at a conference in the historic town of Toledo meant to promote closer business ties with Spain.

Spain, like the United States, wants to see a peaceful transition to democracy and respect for human rights in Cuba, said Ramon de Miguel, Spanish State Secretary for foreign policy and the European Union.
"Spain shares with the U.S. the ultimate aim. In this we do not diverge. We do diverge on the means by which to achieve it," he said.
Miguel, Gardner and Pena were speaking at a news conference. Pena deferred questions on Cuba to the ambassador.
"The American government has employed a commercial embargo. Spain has never practiced this measure," Miguel said.

"To the contrary, this Spanish government and the previous governments have said: Whoever wants to buy, buy. Whoever wants to sell, sell. Whoever wants to invest, invest. This policy has always been the same," he added.

Spain, along with the rest of the European Union, vehemently opposes the U.S. Helms-Burton Act which gives Cuban-Americans the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties seized by the Cuban government from exiles after the 1959 communist revolution.
"We still have a difference with respect to the Helms- Burton legislation," said Gardner.
The European Union has filed a complaint on Helms-Burton with the World Trade Organisation.
"If the opinion (of the WTO) is against extraterritorial practice, surely the American government and its branches must reconsider their position," said Miguel.
Gardner sought to defend the legislation, whose practical implications for foreign companies have been suspended by President Clinton until January.

"The Helms-Burton law does not seek to interfere with trade and investment between Spain and Cuba or between other companies and Cuba except in one very limited respect. It seeks to deal with Spanish or other companies which deal in property stolen from American citizens."
Despite the public discord, Gardner praised Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's new conservative government for taking a tougher line on Cuba than its predecessor.
"We have watched with appreciation as that policy has unfolded in the last months and there is a considerable convergence between the Spanish policy towards Cuba and the United States," Gardner said.
Spain and Cuba have maintained close relations historically and Spain is a leading investor in Cuba.
But Aznar dramatised the hardening attitude of his government at an Ibero-American summit in Chile last week when he said: "I have nothing against Cuba, but everything against its regime."

Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said recently cooperation and aid to Cuba should be linked to political and economic reforms. Spain is urging the European Union to adopt a unified position on Cuba in line with its own policy.
